plants.pruning_notes: No specific pruning requirement identified. As a general guideline for Sacramento, light shaping or removal of dead material in late February to early March suits most plants before the spring growth flush begins.

pruningGuide.rationale: Prune while fully leafless during Sacramento's mild dormant season. Avoids triple-digit summer heat stress after cuts and reduces disease transmission. Structural work is easiest with no foliage.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Remove dead, damaged, or crossing branches. Avoid heavy pruning in summer — Sacramento's 100°F+ days stress trees after cuts.
pruningGuide.examples: Maples, ashes, hackberries, liquidambar, ginkgo, zelkova, pistache, plane trees

pruningGuide.rationale: Fully dormant window in Sacramento. These trees are sensitive to summer heat stress after pruning — timing is critical in the valley.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Minimal pruning is best; natural structure is the appeal. Remove dead or crossing branches only. Never prune in summer heat.
pruningGuide.examples: Acer palmatum cultivars (Bloodgood, Anne Irene, Atropurpureum, etc.)

pruningGuide.rationale: Critical disease-prevention timing. Pruning oaks during the growing season in Sacramento and the Central Valley risks Sudden Oak Death and other fungal pathogens that enter through fresh cuts.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Remove only dead and hazard limbs. Never prune from March through November. Sterilize tools between trees.
pruningGuide.examples: Quercus agrifolia, Q. lobata, Q. kelloggii, Q. suber, Q. ilex, Q. shumardii, Q. virginiana

pruningGuide.rationale: Dormancy window before bud swell. For stone-fruit-family ornamentals, pruning during dormancy minimizes disease entry (e.g., cytospora canker). Sacramento's warm springs mean bud swell can start in late February.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Thin for airflow and light. Avoid late-summer cuts. Redbuds (Cercis) dislike heavy pruning — minimal intervention only.
pruningGuide.examples: Prunus cerasifera, P. serrulata, P. ilicifolia, Cercis canadensis & occidentalis, Chilopsis linearis

pruningGuide.rationale: Before bud swell in Sacramento. Crape myrtles are among the most commonly mistreated trees in Sacramento — topping ('crape murder') is unnecessary and disfiguring.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Selectively remove crossing/rubbing limbs only. Never top. Sacramento's hot summers are ideal for crape myrtles with zero pruning beyond cleanup.
pruningGuide.examples: Lagerstroemia indica 'Acoma'

pruningGuide.rationale: Bottlebrush is not a dormant-season pruner. Prune after its bloom flush in spring. Avoid cutting into old bare wood.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Light shaping and removal of old seed capsules. Heavy cuts into bare wood will not regenerate.
pruningGuide.examples: Callistemon citrinus, C. viminalis 'Hannah Ray'

pruningGuide.rationale: Late February is the optimal window in Sacramento — mild winters mean plants break dormancy early. Waiting past mid-March risks cutting into active growth.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Remove dead/damaged material, lightly shape, clean up winter dieback. Sacramento's warm climate pushes spring growth earlier than most of CA.
pruningGuide.examples: Abelia, Abutilon, Acacia, Arbutus, Dodonaea, Elaeagnus, Escallonia, Euonymus, Nandina, Pittosporum, Rhaphiolepis, Viburnum, and many others

pruningGuide.rationale: Ceanothus must be pruned only after its spring bloom. Pruning into old bare wood kills the plant — it will not regenerate. Minimal intervention is the best approach for long-term health in Sacramento's dry climate.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Light shaping of new growth after bloom only. Never cut into old wood. Avoid all summer pruning.
pruningGuide.examples: Ceanothus griseus, C. maritimus 'Valley Violet', C. thyrsiflorus cultivars

pruningGuide.rationale: Light shaping only after winter/spring bloom. Like Ceanothus, manzanitas will not regenerate from old bare wood — this is a common and fatal mistake in Sacramento landscapes.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Never cut into bare wood. Established manzanitas are extremely drought-tolerant and thrive with minimal intervention.
pruningGuide.examples: Arctostaphylos densiflora cultivars, A. edmundsii, A. manzanita, A. uva-ursi cultivars

pruningGuide.rationale: Prune after the coldest nights have passed but before bud swell, typically January in Sacramento. Airflow is especially critical in Sacramento's dry summers to prevent fungal issues.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Cut to outward-facing buds. Remove dead canes. Open the center for airflow. Deadhead during the season to extend bloom.
pruningGuide.examples: Rosa californica, Rosa rugosa 'Moje Hammarberg'

pruningGuide.rationale: Lady Banks blooms on old wood set the previous season. Pruning in winter removes every flower bud — the plant will not bloom at all that year. Prune only after the spring bloom finishes.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Light thinning only after bloom. Do not prune in winter or early spring.
pruningGuide.examples: Rosa banksiae 'Alba Plena', Rosa banksiae 'Lutea'

pruningGuide.rationale: Two-cut schedule for Sacramento's long season. The July cut removes spent flower stems and lightly shapes after the main flush. The February cut prepares for the new season. Never cut into old bare wood in Sacramento's heat — it may not recover.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Cut back by one-third, never into bare woody stems. Spanish lavender (stoechas) can be sheared after each flush.
pruningGuide.examples: Lavandula angustifolia, L. stoechas 'Anouk' & 'Otto Quast', L. x intermedia cultivars

pruningGuide.rationale: Two cuts work best in Sacramento's long growing season. The July cut removes spent summer flush and encourages fall rebloom — a critical second show in Sacramento. Light February cut tidies winter dieback.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Blooms on new growth so harder cuts are tolerated. Without the July cut, plants get woody and fall bloom declines sharply.
pruningGuide.examples: Salvia greggii 'Autumn Flame', S. greggii 'Furman's Red', S. microphylla 'Killer Cranberry'

pruningGuide.rationale: Mexican sage is a fall bloomer in Sacramento, finishing in November–December. Cut back hard after that bloom ends. Spring pruning is backwards — the plant is budding up for the season and a spring cut sacrifices the entire fall show.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Cut hard to 12–18" in December–January. Plants often stay semi-evergreen in Sacramento's mild winters.
pruningGuide.examples: Salvia leucantha 'Danielle's Dream', S. leucantha 'Midnight'

pruningGuide.rationale: Late-winter tidy before Sacramento's early spring growth flush. Sacramento's mild winters rarely cause severe damage, but a February cleanup promotes vigorous spring growth.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Remove frost-damaged tips. Light shaping only. Most salvias recover quickly from cuts in Sacramento.
pruningGuide.examples: Salvia apiana, S. chamaedryoides, S. clevelandii, S. coccinea, S. spathacea, and others

pruningGuide.rationale: Two-cut schedule is essential. February hard prune (cut side shoots to 2–3 buds) defines structure and forces blooms. July–August cut removes the long whippy summer shoots that, if left, lead to invasive spread in Sacramento's fast-growing climate.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Without the summer cut wisteria can outpace its structure rapidly. Both cuts are necessary for bloom and containment.
pruningGuide.examples: Wisteria floribunda, W. sinensis

pruningGuide.rationale: Prune after Sacramento's frost risk passes (typically by mid-February). Bougainvillea blooms on new wood; harder cuts produce the most dramatic flower display in summer.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Wear gloves — thorns are sharp. Can cut back hard. Avoid pruning in summer heat which stresses the plant.
pruningGuide.examples: Bougainvillea 'Barbara Karst'

pruningGuide.rationale: Blooms on current season's wood. The harder you cut in February, the more vigorous the flowering display during Sacramento's long warm summers.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Cut back hard to 12–18". Deadhead spent spikes during the season to extend bloom into fall.
pruningGuide.examples: Buddleja davidii White Profusion

pruningGuide.rationale: Vitex blooms on new growth — a hard February cut encourages the most flower spikes. Sacramento's hot summers produce outstanding vitex bloom when the plant has been cut back well.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Can cut back to a low framework annually, or deadhead spent spikes for a second flush.
pruningGuide.examples: Vitex agnus-castus

pruningGuide.rationale: Lantana acts as a perennial in Sacramento. Cut back hard while dormant in December–February — cutting in spring (as the original database had it) means cutting into actively growing plants and sacrificing early-season bloom.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Cut to 6–12". Promotes fresh vigorous growth and best flowering the following summer.
pruningGuide.examples: Lantana hybrids, L. montevidensis 'Alba', L. hybrid 'Carnival'

pruningGuide.rationale: Blooms on old wood — any pruning before bloom removes flower buds. Prune immediately after the spring bloom finishes. Avoid heavy cuts that expose wood to Sacramento's intense summer sun.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Light shaping only after bloom. Do not prune in winter.
pruningGuide.examples: Camellia japonica 'April Kiss'

pruningGuide.rationale: All bloom on old wood. Prune after blooming finishes. In Sacramento, a May–June shape suits both types. Light thinning maintains an open, airy form that handles summer heat better.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Deadhead spent flowers. Light shaping only — never cut into old wood. Heavy pruning in Sacramento's heat stresses these plants.
pruningGuide.examples: Camellia sasanqua 'Alabama Beauty', Rhododendron spp.

pruningGuide.rationale: Blooms on old wood in late winter/early spring. Pruning before or during bloom removes all flowers. Remove one-third of the oldest canes after bloom to encourage new flowering wood.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Do not prune in winter or early spring. Remove old canes at the base rather than shearing.
pruningGuide.examples: Forsythia x intermedia 'Gold Tide'

pruningGuide.rationale: Type determines timing. Bigleaf (macrophylla) blooms on old wood — remove only dead stems in November–December. Panicle (paniculata) blooms on new wood — prune hard in January–February. Sacramento's mild winters mean frost damage to cuts is minimal.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Identify the type before pruning. Pruning bigleaf in winter eliminates all blooms. Panicle types tolerate and benefit from hard cuts.
pruningGuide.examples: Hydrangea spp.

pruningGuide.rationale: Cut back to the ground after the first frost. In Sacramento, this is typically November. Hostas are fully dormant through the mild Sacramento winter.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: No pruning needed at any other time of year. Fully dormant in winter.
pruningGuide.examples: Hosta spp.

pruningGuide.rationale: Sacramento's warm springs push ornamental grasses into active growth early — don't wait past mid-March. Cut back before new growth emerges from the base.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Cut back to 4–6 inches. Carex and sedges: 3–4 inches. Festuca can go summer-dormant in Sacramento's heat — late winter cut refreshes for spring.
pruningGuide.examples: Muhlenbergia, Miscanthus, Pennisetum, Nassella, Bouteloua, Festuca, Carex, Juncus, Chondropetalum

pruningGuide.rationale: Light shaping only before new growth. In Sacramento avoid all summer pruning — heat combined with fresh cuts stresses conifers significantly.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Never cut into old wood. Conifers will not regenerate from bare stems. Light tip shaping only.
pruningGuide.examples: Cedrus, Cupressus, Juniperus, Pinus, Podocarpus, Thuja, Hesperocyparis, Sequoiadendron

pruningGuide.rationale: Either timing works in Sacramento's mild winters. November–December cut is tidier; February–March cut leaves stems for winter interest and some frost protection. Cut back to basal growth before new shoots emerge.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Both windows are valid — choose based on aesthetics. Watch for early spring emergence in Sacramento (late February) and cut before new growth gets going.
pruningGuide.examples: Achillea, Agastache, Amsonia, Anemone, Aster, Coreopsis, Dietes, Hemerocallis, Iris, Lavandula (intermedia), Nepeta, Penstemon, Salvia clevelandii, Tagetes lemmonii, Tulbaghia, and many others

pruningGuide.rationale: Lightly shape after any late-winter bloom flush. Rosemary is extremely drought-tolerant in Sacramento's dry climate and thrives with minimal pruning.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Avoid cutting into old woody stems. Light shaping of new growth only.
pruningGuide.examples: Rosmarinus officinalis cultivars (Chef's Choice, Blue Spires, Ken Taylor, Prostratus, Tuscan Blue)

pruningGuide.rationale: Prune after harvest (fruit typically ripens October–November in Sacramento). February–March works well before new growth. Can be trained as hedge or espalier.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Avoid removing too much fruiting wood. Light shaping; responds well to training.
pruningGuide.examples: Acca sellowiana

pruningGuide.rationale: Prune after leaf drop through February. Figs are vigorous and can be cut back hard in Sacramento. Avoid summer pruning — cuts bleed heavily and stress the tree in the heat.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Can cut back hard to control size. Remove crossing or inward-facing branches.
pruningGuide.examples: Ficus carica

pruningGuide.rationale: Prune before new growth in February–March. Thin canopy for light penetration. Removing interior branches also reduces fruit production if desired for clean-up reasons.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Can be shaped as standard tree or multi-trunk. Avoid summer pruning.
pruningGuide.examples: Olea europaea (standard); Olea europaea 'Little Ollie' (dwarf shrub form) — same timing

pruningGuide.rationale: Prune while fully dormant. Sacramento's hot dry summers make open canopy structure important for fruit quality and to prevent sunburn on interior wood.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Remove suckers at the base. Thin crossing branches and open the canopy. Light intervention for dwarf forms.
pruningGuide.examples: Punica granatum 'Angel Red', P. granatum 'Nana'

pruningGuide.rationale: Prune after the risk of frost passes in Sacramento (usually by early March). Citrus is frost-sensitive — cutting before the last frost exposes tender new growth. Minimal pruning needed; citrus are naturally well-shaped.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Remove dead wood, crossing branches, and suckers below the graft. Avoid heavy pruning that removes fruiting wood.
pruningGuide.examples: Citrus aurantifolia (lime), Citrus × paradisi (grapefruit), Fortunella spp. (kumquat)

pruningGuide.rationale: Remove dead or damaged leaves and spent flower stalks in early spring before Sacramento's heat sets in. Minimal intervention is best — these plants are well-adapted to Sacramento valley conditions.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Remove only dead material and spent flower stalks. Avoid heavy pruning. Agaves are monocarpic (die after flowering) — remove the spent spike.
pruningGuide.examples: Agave, Aloe, Echeveria, Sedum, Sempervivum, Dudleya, Opuntia, Echinopsis, Hesperaloe, Mangave

pruningGuide.rationale: Remove dead or brown fronds in early spring. Sacramento's hot dry summers are stressful; excessive frond removal (hurricane cuts) weakens palms and reduces their ability to handle heat.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Leave all green fronds intact. Remove only brown/dead fronds. Never hurricane-cut palms.
pruningGuide.examples: Chamaerops humilis 'Cerifera', Cycas revoluta, Trachycarpus wagnerianus

pruningGuide.rationale: Cut back old fronds before new growth emerges. In Sacramento's mild winters, fronds often stay semi-green — remove only truly dead material.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Cut back to the base. New fronds will emerge from the crown in spring.
pruningGuide.examples: Cyrtomium falcatum, Polypodium californicum, Polystichum munitum, Woodwardia areolata

pruningGuide.rationale: Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom — it feeds the bulb for the following year. In Sacramento's warm spring, foliage typically matures by May–June for spring bulbs.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Never cut foliage until fully yellow. Remove spent flower heads if desired. Iris: trim fans to 6–8" in July–August; divide every 3–4 years in August.
pruningGuide.examples: Allium, Amaryllis belladonna, Bletilla, Narcissus, Sternbergia, Iris (bearded & Pacific Coast), spring bulbs

pruningGuide.rationale: No scheduled pruning required. Remove spent plants at end of season. Deadhead during the season to prolong bloom.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Remove spent plants at end of their growing cycle. No structured pruning schedule needed.
pruningGuide.examples: Calibrachoa, Diascia, Eschscholzia (CA poppy), Helianthus annuus

pruningGuide.rationale: Most California natives prefer minimal pruning in Sacramento's hot valley climate. Heavy cutting removes the structure that provides shade and cooling. Light shaping after bloom is preferred.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Remove dead wood and lightly shape after bloom. Monkeyflower: cut back by half after first flush in May–June, again in August.
pruningGuide.examples: Diplacus aurantiacus, Encelia californica, Lupinus albifrons, Epilobium, Zauschneria, Ribes

pruningGuide.rationale: Post-bloom foliage trimming in July–August reduces disease and water loss during Sacramento's long hot dry summers. Trim fans to 6–8". Divide overcrowded clumps every 3–4 years in August.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Cut flower stalks to the base after bloom. Trim fans in July–August. Remove dead foliage in November.
pruningGuide.examples: Iris x germanica, Iris bearded cultivars, Iris Pacific Coast hybrids, Iris douglasiana

pruningGuide.rationale: Pruning group determines timing. Group 3 (summer/fall bloomers) push growth fast in Sacramento's warm spring — prune to 12–18" in February before bud break.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Identify the pruning group before cutting. Group 3: hard cut Feb. Groups 1–2: light cut after first bloom flush only.
pruningGuide.examples: Clematis spp.

pruningGuide.rationale: Prune after frost risk passes in Sacramento (mid-February). Blooms on new growth tips — cutting promotes the most flowers for the coming season.
pruningGuide.crew_notes: Can cut to main framework for dramatic shape, or lightly tip-prune for a larger plant.
pruningGuide.examples: Brugmansia spp.
